<explanation>
The Libwebsockets project is a modular, highly configurable C library that supports a range of communication protocols (HTTP/1, HTTP/2, WebSockets, MQTT, etc.) and provides both “low‐level” wsi functionality as well as a higher-level Secure Streams (SS) abstraction. In creating your system design diagram, consider separating the entire project into logical layers and subsystems. Here’s how you can break it down and what to include:

1. Main Components to Represent:
 a. Core Engine & Context Management – Represent the base “lib/core” and “lib/system” components that implement connection state, event handling, and resource management.
 b. Protocol Implementations – Include distinct modules for HTTP (roles/h1, roles/h2, roles/http), WebSockets (roles/ws), MQTT (roles/mqtt) and other protocol-specific logic.
 c. Secure Streams (SS) Layer – A higher-level abstraction sitting on top of the raw connections, defined in the “lib/secure-streams” section. Also include serialized secure streams and the SS Proxy component (ssproxy) to show how it abstractly manages policy, retries, and multiplexing.
 d. TLS & Crypto Abstraction – Show the “lib/tls” subsystem which supports various TLS providers (OpenSSL, MbedTLS, etc.) and the cryptographic modules (e.g., in lib/cose, lib/jose) that work with crypto protocols.
 e. Event Loop Integration – Indicate the event libraries and schedulers (lib/event-libs) that support multiple runtimes (libuv, libev, glib, etc. as well as custom event libs) through directional arrows feeding into the core loop.
 f. Platform & Driver Abstraction – Diagram the “lib/plat” and “lib/drivers” sections. These help bridge to platform-specific network I/O, timer, file, and hardware driver layers (like for FreeRTOS, POSIX, Windows, or embedded platforms).
 g. Policy & Configuration – Emphasize the JSON-based “policy” portion that drives, for example, the vhost, secure streams settings, TLS validation details, connection retry/backoff, and protocol negotiation. This is key in the SS layer where endpoint, protocol, and metadata information are centralized.
 h. Sample Applications and Plugins – Represent how minimal examples (in minimal-examples, test-apps) and plugins (both standalone and in the “plugins” folder) use the library. Indicate that these serve as both integration tests and “client/server” demonstrations.

2. Relationships and Interactions:
 • Use directional arrows to indicate how the application (or plugin) code interacts with the core engine.
 • Show the secure streams layer as connecting upward from the low-level wsi APIs. Emphasize that policy JSON input drives SS behavior on top of the core connection management.
 • Illustrate how the event loops feed events into the core processing, and that TLS (and crypto) modules attach to every connection for security handling.
 • Depict the platform abstraction layer as bridging the OS/hardware differences and providing uniform interfaces to the core.

3. Design Patterns and Patterns to Highlight:
 • Modular design: the project is built in logical “modules” (or libraries) that can be independently built and configured using CMake.
 • Separation of concerns: from low-level connection handling (wsi) to higher-level secure streams abstraction – with policy files governing behavior.
 • Event-driven architecture: multiple event loop integrations are supported; display a central “event scheduler” receiving I/O events and dispatching them to protocol handlers.
 • Configurability through JSON: show that many parameters (connection endpoints, TLS settings, retry policies) are externalized into policy files for both runtime adaptation and easy configuration.
 • Portability: illustrate separate branches for platform-specific implementations, such as within lib/plat for UNIX, Windows, FreeRTOS, etc.

4. Technologies, Frameworks, and Tools:
 • CMake is used for building across platforms.
 • Multiple crypto libraries (MbedTLS, OpenSSL) as indicated in lib/tls.
 • Several event loop libraries (libuv, libev, glib, etc.) and plugins provide integration.
 • The diagram should also list examples such as generic “secure streams proxy” components and embedded examples (like those found in embedded/ and minimal-examples).

5. Diagram Layout Guidelines for this Project:
 • Use clear, labeled boxes for each main component: “Core”, “Protocols”, “Secure Streams”, “TLS & Crypto”, “Event Loop Integration”, and “Platform Drivers/Abstraction”.
 • Draw arrows to show data flow and dependency directions – for instance, arrows going from Secure Streams down to the core, and from the core to the TLS modules.
 • Consider using color coding or distinct shapes to differentiate between core library modules, platform-specific adapters, and user-level examples/plugins.
 • If desired, include an inset that shows the legacy “low-level” wsi path versus the Secure Streams path to illustrate the evolution of the architecture.
 • Label the JSON policy file as a central configuration artifact that feeds into the secure streams layer.

6. Extra Detail:
 • Include subcomponents from directories such as “lib/drivers” (button, led, netdev, etc.) and “lib/event-libs” (showing different supported event libraries).
 • Optionally note that testing (CI and test-apps) and auxiliary scripts (in scripts/) support the development and build process but are not part of the runtime architecture.

By creating a diagram that clearly separates each layer and shows the interactions between the event loop, core connection management, TLS/crypto, secure streams abstraction, and protocol drivers, you provide a comprehensive view of how Libwebsockets works from bottom (platform I/O) to top (user-facing APIs and plugins). The use of clear labels, directional arrows, distinct colors or shapes, and annotations regarding JSON-configured policies will help capture all the essential architectural elements for a principal software engineer’s review.
</explanation>
